English_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Kamma 17a: ‘Rabba bar bar Ḥana said: I was once walking together with Rabbi Yoḥanan to ask him about this statement. Whenever he would enter a lavatory, upon his exit I would ask him to explain a matter, and he would not answer us until he had washed his hands and donned his phylacteries and made the blessing, and only then would he answer us. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And how could it ever enter the mind that it was for their detriment? Rather, one might think it better that man depend in every moment upon Hashem to enlighten him how to act, without a fixed code like the Shulchan Arukh directing his path, which might reduce his constant yearning for Hashem. But in truth it is for your benefit, providing a radiant light upon which to lean, whereas without the Torah one would stand in perpetual terror in every deed lest he be mistaken and it not be the true will of Hashem.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And he said to the woman: Yea, has God said: You shall not eat of every tree of the garden? The essence of the serpent tempting her by stating that Hashem's command applied to all trees of the garden not to eat, was because such is indeed the truth: for through the protective fence placed upon this single tree, a boundary automatically extended over the entire garden that he not eat of it except according to the will of Hashem, blessed be He; for so it is likewise among Israel: once forbidden foods are prohibited unto them, restraint is automatically required when necessary even concerning permitted things.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: If so, Balaam too must outwardly have been free of all these defects and capable of teaching the way of the Blessed One, in a manner resembling our father Abraham, peace be upon him; for he was a prophet to God and knew the truth of the Blessed One, as his prophecy was true prophecy recorded in the Torah. Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As in Tikkunim and Zohar: “Come, let us deal wisely with them” (Exodus 1:10) parallels “Come, let us build us a city.” For Nimrod’s Tower, Nebuchadnezzar’s golden idol, and Pharaoh’s store-cities all share one character: seeking to compel divine bounty through spiritual manipulation, refusing to humble themselves under holiness; refusing the arduous toil of self-restraint, wishing to luxuriate in worldly lusts while remaining immune from divine retribution.
